strengths: The core observation is crisp and correct: for binary-reward tasks, RL on expected reward optimizes pass@1 while maximum likelihood optimizes log pass rate, and log p admits a Maclaurin expansion as a harmonic mixture of pass@k gradients (Eq. 4-5). This gives a clean, population-level way to see RL as a first-order approximation of ML.

Theorem 2 is elegant: the simple estimator that averages score functions over successful rollouts only (normalize by K instead of N) is exactly unbiased for the truncated ML objective of order T=N, so more sampling compute provably improves the target objective itself, not just estimation variance. This estimator–objective equivalence is a genuinely useful result and the proof (Appendix B) is correct and short.

The method reduces to a one-line change to the advantage computation relative to GRPO/RLOO (Algorithm 1), making it trivially adoptable, and the control-variate derivation for variance reduction (Eq. 10) handles the subtlety that K is random and correlated with the rollouts.

The unifying weight-function view (Section 5, Table 2, Figure 1) is a valuable analytical contribution: it cleanly characterizes REINFORCE, GRPO, MaxRL, and ML by their per-input weighting w(p), reinterprets GRPO's std-normalization as 1/sqrt(p(1-p)) weighting (consistent with Davis and Recht 2025), and explains why GRPO fails to interpolate toward ML with more compute.

Experiments are unusually thorough across regimes: (i) a controlled ImageNet setting where exact ML is available and MaxRL is shown to converge to cross-entropy as rollouts increase while REINFORCE stalls (Figure 2, 8, 9); (ii) an effectively infinite-data maze setting; (iii) a data-scarce GSM8K regime with 50 epochs showing reduced pass@k degradation; and (iv) large-scale Qwen3-1.7B/4B RLVR training on POLARIS-53K with consistent Pareto dominance over GRPO and up to ~20x test-time scaling efficiency gains. Comparisons include strong recent baselines (PKPO, differential smoothing, entropy-bonus GRPO), not just vanilla GRPO.

Limitations are discussed honestly (binary rewards only, no continuous/multi-turn/off-policy extension yet), and the paper carefully delineates its contributions from the closely related Xiong et al. (2025b) and Davis and Recht (2025).
Hyperparameters, prompts, and implementation details (verl-based, fully on-policy, no KL or entropy bonuses for the main comparison) are documented in sufficient depth to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate relative to concurrent/prior work. The success-conditioned estimator (averaging score functions over successful trajectories) is essentially rejection-fine-tuning/RAFT-style training with a mean baseline, and the connection between such procedures and log-like weighting of pass rate is already established by Davis and Recht (2025); Xiong et al. (2025b) also optimizes non-linear functions of pass rate. The genuinely new pieces are the finite-N estimator–objective equivalence and the compute-indexed Maclaurin family, which the paper states clearly, but the conceptual delta is incremental.

The 'increasing compute improves the objective' framing is somewhat rhetorical: the target objective changes with the rollout budget N (J^(N) is a different objective for each N), and whether maximizing log pass rate rather than expected reward is the right practitioner goal is asserted more than established (the ImageNet experiment supports it, but it is by construction a supervised classification setting where cross-entropy is known to be superior).

For prompts with very low pass rate, the advantage normalization by mean reward (effectively a 1/p weighting) implies high-variance updates on the hardest inputs; the paper analyzes variance qualitatively and adds a control variate but does not report stability/ablation of this weighting (e.g., clipping or capping w(p)) at LLM scale, where only N=16 rollouts are used.

All large-scale LLM experiments are on a single domain (mathematical reasoning with a perfect verifier). The abstract's claim that MaxRL 'Pareto-dominates existing methods in all models and tasks we tested' is accurate for the tested settings, but generalization to other correctness-based domains (code, Lean, multi-turn) is left to future work, so the scope of the empirical claims should be read as math-RLVR.

Some minor presentation issues: text refers to Equation (9) when discussing unbiasedness of (9) vs the estimator, the estimator notation g_N vs the K=0 convention requires careful reading, and the '20x' headline figure is the maximum over many benchmark/model pairs rather than a typical case.

GRPO comparisons are made in a fully on-policy, single-gradient-step regime where GRPO's known clipping/off-policy machinery is inactive; while this is a fair objective-level comparison and entropy-bonus and PKPO variants are included, practitioners using PPO-style multi-epoch setups may see smaller gaps.

strengths: The core theoretical observation is clean and useful: expressing J_ML as a Maclaurin series in fail@k (Eq. 4-5) cleanly shows that expected-reward RL optimizes only the first-order term, and yields a compute-indexed family of objectives interpolating between REINFORCE and exact maximum likelihood.

Theorem 2 provides an exact estimator-objective equivalence at each finite rollout count N, which is a genuinely nice alignment: the simple change of normalizing by successful samples K rather than N makes additional rollouts improve the target objective itself rather than only reducing variance. The proofs (Appendix B) are correct and short.

The weight-function view (Section 5, Appendix C) gives an interpretable population-level comparison of REINFORCE, GRPO, MaxRL, and ML, and usefully explains GRPO's pass@k degradation as an induced-objective property rather than an implementation artifact.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for an objective-level paper: a controlled setting with exact ML (ImageNet), a procedural maze environment with compute scaling, a multi-epoch GSM8K regime isolating overfitting/diversity collapse, and billion-parameter Qwen3 training on math reasoning with 8 evaluation benchmarks, plus comparison against PKPO, differential smoothing, entropy bonuses, and SELF in the smaller-scale settings.

The paper is honest about its relationship to closely related concurrent work (Davis and Recht, 2025; Xiong et al., 2025b; Nguyen et al., 2025b) and about limitations (binary rewards only, on-policy only, K=0 handling).
weaknesses: The algorithmic contribution is small: the method amounts to a one-line change to the advantage normalization (divide by group mean reward instead of by N or by std). Given the acknowledged overlap with Davis and Recht (2025) (same success-conditioned gradient observation) and Xiong et al. (2025b) (non-linear pass-rate weighting), the marginal novelty over the concurrent literature is limited, and the paper is best viewed as consolidating and empirically validating an idea that is 'in the air'.

There is a subtle mismatch between theory and the implemented algorithm. Theorem 2 establishes unbiasedness for the estimator in Eq. (9)/(10), but Algorithm 1 additionally drops the control-variate term when K=0 ('this choice is simpler and performs better empirically'), so the deployed algorithm is not the unbiased estimator analyzed. The resulting objective being optimized in the K=0 case is not characterized; this weakens the 'unbiased estimator' framing that the headline claims rest on.

The GRPO weight-function analysis (Appendix C) uses the population variance of a Bernoulli variable, whereas practical GRPO uses the empirical standard deviation with an epsilon in the denominator, which behaves quite differently (e.g., when all samples in a group succeed or fail). The claimed 1/sqrt(p(1-p)) weighting is therefore an idealization, and the GRPO 'inversion for large p' conclusion inherits this idealization.

Headline empirical claims are stronger than the evidence. 'Pareto-dominates existing methods in all models and tasks we tested' and 'up to 20x test-time scaling gains' rest partly on GRPO's known pass@k degradation relative to base models; at the large scale (Qwen3), the only baseline is GRPO - PKPO and differential smoothing, which MaxRL beats at small scale, are not run at 1.7B/4B. No seeds, error bars, or variance across runs are reported in the main text for any LLM experiment.

The heavy 1/p weighting toward hard prompts is acknowledged qualitatively (Figure 6: large gradient norms near zero pass rate) but potential downsides - instability, sensitivity to noisy verifiers (all experiments use a perfect verifier), and interaction with label noise on GSM8K-style data - are not analyzed. The strong-verifier assumption is stated only in passing, yet most of the claimed practical benefit (20x inference efficiency with a perfect verifier) depends on it.

Reproducibility is incomplete as submitted: the project website/code footnote is empty in the manuscript, and while hyperparameters are given in appendices, key implementation details (e.g., the modified rollout engine in verl, maze generation protocol) would be hard to replicate exactly without the code release.

Writing has recurring grammatical errors ('MaxRL show better scaling', 'we study how MaxRL behave', 'MaxRL match or ourperform', 'GRPO-trained models at the highest compute similarly trail'), and the 'Takeaway' boxes restate figure captions without adding analysis, which slightly inflates the presentation.

strengths: The core theoretical contribution is correct, clean, and verifiable: the Maclaurin expansion of log p in terms of fail@k (Eq. 4), the resulting gradient identity over pass@k terms (Eq. 5), and Theorem 2 showing the simple success-only REINFORCE estimator is exactly unbiased for the order-T=N truncated objective. The estimator-objective equivalence is elegant and directly supports the central claim that additional sampling compute improves the optimized objective itself rather than just reducing variance.

The weight-function view (Section 5, Appendix C) is a genuinely useful unifying lens: it cleanly characterizes REINFORCE (w=1), GRPO (w=1/sqrt(p(1-p))), MaxRL, and ML (w=1/p) at the population level, explains GRPO's inversion at high pass rates, and situates the method relative to pass@k-optimization approaches.

The experimental program is unusually thorough and well-designed: a controlled ImageNet setting where exact ML is implementable (validating the convergence-to-ML claim), an infinite-data maze regime isolating compute scaling, a data-scarce GSM8K regime isolating overfitting/diversity degradation, and billion-scale Qwen3 training on math benchmarks. Comparisons include not only GRPO/RLOO but also PKPO, differential smoothing, SELF, and entropy-bonus variants.

The empirical findings are substantive and practically relevant: consistent pass@k preservation relative to base models where GRPO collapses, large test-time scaling efficiency gains (up to ~20x with a perfect verifier), and mechanistic analyses (gradient norms vs. pass rate, fraction of prompts with non-zero pass rate) that connect the population-level theory to observed training dynamics.

Related work treatment is honest and careful: the paper explicitly delineates its contribution from Davis and Recht (2025), Xiong et al. (2025b), RAFT/STaR-style rejection fine-tuning, and pass@k objectives (shown to be a special case), rather than overclaiming novelty.

Limitations are candidly discussed (binary rewards only, single-line estimator deviation causing bias when K=0, GRPO inversion conjecture left to future work), and hyperparameters/implementation details are documented extensively in appendices.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the success-conditioned expectation (Theorem 1) and the estimator (Eq. 9) are closely connected to known rejection fine-tuning / STaR / RAFT-style training and to recent observations by Davis and Recht (2025) and Xiong et al. (2025b). The distinct contribution is the finite-compute estimator-objective equivalence and interpolation framing, which is real but incremental relative to that closely related work.

Variance is not analyzed theoretically. The estimator normalizes by the random variable K, and when pass rates are low the 1/K factor can produce very large gradient magnitudes (visible in Figure 6); the paper relies entirely on empirical stability and a single control variate without bounds or a variance comparison against REINFORCE/GRPO at matched compute.

Several universal claims outrun the evidence: 'Pareto-dominates existing methods in all models and tasks we tested' and the abstract's 20x figure rest on single-run experiments without error bars, seeds, or statistical significance reporting, and on a fixed set of math/code-style correctness tasks; generalization beyond verifiable binary-reward domains is untested.

Reproducibility is weakened by an empty project/code link (footnote 1 is a placeholder) in the manuscript; while hyperparameters are detailed, the implementation requires nontrivial modifications to verl's rollout engine that are only briefly described.

Compute accounting between methods could be tighter: comparisons at fixed RL step counts with different rollout counts conflate gradient-step and rollout-compute budgets in some plots, and the practical implications of the T=N coupling (large-scale experiments effectively use T=16, a low approximation order) deserve more discussion.

The implementation (Algorithm 1) deviates from the analyzed estimator (scaling by N, dropping updates when K=0, which introduces bias); this is acknowledged, but the gap between the unbiasedness guarantees and the deployed algorithm is left unquantified.

strengths: Clean and elegant theoretical framing: the Maclaurin expansion of the log-pass-rate in terms of pass@k events, and the estimator–objective equivalence (Theorem 2), is an exact and satisfying result showing that the proposed one-line change (normalizing by successful samples K instead of total samples N) targets a compute-indexed family of objectives interpolating between REINFORCE and maximum likelihood. Theorem 5's careful analysis showing the practical estimator is unbiased for order T = N − 1 (not T = N) reflects unusual technical honesty.

The unifying weight-function view (Section 5, Table 2, Figure 1) that characterizes RL, GRPO, MaxRL, and ML by a scalar weighting of pass rate is insightful and provides a clear mechanistic explanation for GRPO's distribution-sharpening behavior and MaxRL's emphasis on hard prompts.

Comprehensive, well-structured empirical evaluation across four regimes: a controlled ImageNet setting where exact ML (cross-entropy) is implementable as an upper bound, an infinite-data maze setting, a data-scarce GSM8K multi-epoch setting, and large-scale Qwen3-1.7B/4B reasoning training. Baseline coverage is unusually broad (RLOO, GRPO, entropy-bonus GRPO, PKPO, ZPD, Power Function, Differential Smoothing, SELF), and the ablations (gradient norms, non-zero-pass-rate fraction, per-prompt pass-rate distributions, SNR, control-variate variance analysis, non-binary reward extension) directly support the mechanistic claims.

The ImageNet experiment with exact cross-entropy as ground truth is a particularly strong validation: it demonstrates that MaxRL converges to ML as rollout compute increases, while REINFORCE stalls — directly testing the core theoretical claim rather than only relative benchmark wins.

Honest limitations discussion (binary rewards only, zero gradient for prompts with no successful rollout, incomplete theoretical treatment of non-binary rewards) and strong reproducibility: open-sourced code, detailed hyperparameters, prompts, and training setups in appendices.

Practical significance: the method is a one-line modification to standard GRPO-style advantage computation, making it trivially adoptable, and the pass@k improvements address the well-documented distribution-sharpening/pass@k degradation problem in RLVR.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty in isolation: Theorem 1 is a straightforward conditional-expectation identity (essentially a likelihood-ratio/Rao-Blackwellization step), and the paper itself acknowledges that Davis and Recht (2025) made a similar observation and that Xiong et al. (2025b) consider related non-linear pass-rate objectives. The main contribution is the exact finite-compute estimator–objective equivalence and its empirical consequences, which is valuable but incremental relative to this concurrent work.

The headline claim of 'up to 20× test-time scaling efficiency gains over GRPO' relies on a perfect-verifier best-of-k setting, which inflates practical relevance; the majority-voting (verifier-free) gains in Table 7, while consistent, are more modest.

The estimator inherits a well-known limitation: no gradient when K = 0, so very hard prompts (p ≈ 0) with limited rollout budgets receive zero signal, the very regime the log weighting is intended to emphasize. The paper acknowledges this but the interaction between low N and the 1/p-style amplification (variance/instability) is only analyzed empirically.

The argument that ML is 'the principled objective' for these tasks is asserted more than proven; whether log-likelihood weighting of hard prompts is optimal (vs. e.g., pass@k objectives like PKPO's tuned T) is contested in the literature, and the reported finding that MaxRL beats PKPO at PKPO's own optimized metric is only hypothesized rather than explained.
No comparison with RS-GRPO (Jiang et al., 2026), which the paper identifies as closely related prior work on diversity during LLM reasoning training; this is a notable baseline gap.

Experiments are restricted to binary verifiable-reward reasoning-style tasks plus one didactic classification task; generalization to multi-turn, continuous-reward, or off-policy (PPO-style) settings is deferred to future work, limiting the scope of the conclusion that 'some limitations of RL arise from objective choice.'

strengths: Clean and elegant core insight: the simple normalization change (divide by successful-sample count K rather than total samples N) yields an estimator whose expectation is provably the gradient of a truncated maximum-likelihood objective (Theorem 2), establishing an exact estimator-objective correspondence at each finite rollout budget. The compute-indexed family of objectives interpolating between REINFORCE and exact ML is a genuinely useful conceptual framing.

The unifying weight-function view (Section 5, Table 2, Figure 1) cleanly characterizes REINFORCE, GRPO, MaxRL, and ML at the population level and yields a non-obvious reinterpretation of GRPO (its weighting inverts for high pass rates), connecting to the distribution-sharpening literature.

Unusually broad and well-designed empirical evaluation: a controlled ImageNet setting where exact ML (cross-entropy) is implementable as ground truth, a procedurally generated infinite-data maze setting, a data-scarce GSM8K setting, and large-scale Qwen3-1.7B/4B reasoning training; comparisons against RLOO, GRPO, PKPO, ZPD, entropy-bonused GRPO, differential smoothing, and power-function weighting, plus careful variance and gradient-norm analyses.

The experimental design is thoughtful: showing MaxRL converges to cross-entropy as rollout compute increases (Figure 2), demonstrating PKPO explicitly optimizing pass@T is still beaten at pass@T, and the per-prompt pass-rate distribution analysis (Figure 14) that directly visualizes the sharpening mechanism.

Honest limitations discussion (binary rewards only, zero-gradient for unsolved prompts, the T=N-1 vs T=N subtlety of the practical estimator) and a clear code/asset release plan; the Appendix D analysis of the practical estimator's effective truncation order is a nice touch of rigor.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty relative to concurrent work. Theorem 1 (conditional form of the ML gradient) is essentially the ratio-of-gradients identity and the paper itself concedes Davis and Recht (2025) made a similar observation; the Maclaurin-expansion derivation is elementary. The main intellectual payload reduces to recognizing that a one-line normalization change targets a different population objective, which is close in spirit to difficulty-reweighting methods already in the literature (Xiong et al., 2025b; PopArt-style normalization; RLOO mean baseline).

The 'emphasizes hard inputs' narrative is partially undercut by the method itself: prompts with zero successful rollouts in N samples receive exactly zero gradient on average, so the very hardest inputs (p < 1/N) that ML weighting should amplify most are entirely silent. This is acknowledged but under-explored relative to how central the claim is to the paper's motivation.

The population-level GRPO analysis (Appendix E) assumes the true Bernoulli standard deviation in the denominator; empirical GRPO uses batch estimates, so the derived weight function w(p) = 1/sqrt(p(1-p)) is an idealization, and conclusions drawn from Figure 1 (e.g., the weighting inversion for easy prompts) inherit this gap.

Headline claims ('up to 20× test-time scaling efficiency gains over GRPO') rely on a perfect-verifier repeated-sampling setting and the best across 8 configurations; the framing is favorable, and average-case gains across benchmarks are substantially smaller (e.g., 2.3×-7.9× in several panels).

The ImageNet REINFORCE comparison is close to a strawman: training from a random initialization with ~0.1% pass rate is a known pathological regime for REINFORCE, and the paper admits this caveat only in an appendix footnote, yet Figure 2 is presented as a main result.

Practical reach is bounded: binary rewards only (non-binary extension in M.4 is preliminary, one environment, no theory), fully on-policy with no importance-sampling machinery, and the largest-scale runs use modest budgets (1000 RL steps, 16 rollouts, 4B models) relative to modern RLVR practice, so the compute-scaling story is extrapolated rather than demonstrated at frontier scale.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and clearly articulated: RL on binary terminal rewards optimizes E[p] while maximum likelihood optimizes E[log p], and the Maclaurin expansion of log p in pass@k events (Eq. 4-5) gives a principled compute-indexed family of objectives interpolating between the two.

The estimator-objective equivalence (Theorem 2) is a genuinely nice result: dividing by successful samples K rather than total samples N means that increasing rollout compute improves the optimized objective itself rather than merely reducing variance. The companion analysis (Theorem 5) showing the practical implementation is unbiased for order T = N-1 is an honest and careful treatment of the gap between theory and the deployed estimator.

The unifying weight-function view (Section 5, Table 2, Figure 1) is a valuable conceptual contribution: it characterizes RL, GRPO, MaxRL, and ML as a single family differing only in pass-rate weighting, and yields the interesting observation that GRPO's weighting inverts for easy inputs (p -> 1).

Empirical evaluation is unusually thorough and well-matched to the claims: a controlled ImageNet setting where exact ML is implementable (validating convergence to cross-entropy as rollouts scale), an infinite-data maze regime, a data-scarce GSM8K regime, and billion-parameter Qwen3-4B training on standard math benchmarks. Comparisons go well beyond RLOO/GRPO to include PKPO, ZPD, Power Function weighting, differential smoothing, and entropy bonuses, and MaxRL wins consistently including on metrics its competitors directly optimize (e.g., beating PKPO at pass@16).

Mechanistic analyses (gradient norms vs. pass rate, pass-rate distribution sharpening, non-zero signal fraction, SNR scaling, majority-voting and per-problem solvability on AIME) give real insight into *why* the method works rather than just reporting wins.

Reproducibility is strong: complete hyperparameters for every setting, open-sourced code, prompt templates, and honest discussion of the baseline/truncation subtleties and the zero-gradient-for-failed-prompts limitation. Limitations (binary rewards, no off-policy/PPO setting) are candidly stated.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate. The paper itself acknowledges that Davis and Recht (2025) made a similar conditional-gradient observation and that Xiong et al. (2025b) considered non-linear pass-rate objectives; Theorem 1 is essentially an elementary conditional-expectation identity, and the resulting estimator is a one-line change (normalization by K instead of N) with connections to RWR/AWR forward-KL objectives. The value of the paper rests mainly on the formal finite-N equivalence and the empirical validation, which are solid but not groundbreaking.

Scope is restricted to binary terminal-reward (verifiable correctness) settings. The paper concedes this, and the non-binary extension in Appendix M.4 is preliminary (a single modified maze experiment with no theoretical treatment), so the strong claims in the abstract ('Pareto-dominates existing methods in all tested models and tasks') should be read as scoped to correctness-based domains only.

The estimator's variance behavior when K is small (division by a random, possibly small K) is a real practical concern for low-pass-rate prompts; the baseline/control-variate analysis in Appendix M.2 is empirical rather than providing any variance bound, and the strongest theoretical guarantees are effectively limited to prompts with at least one success.

Several headline results (e.g., pass@k improvements over the base model, the 20x test-time scaling gains under a perfect verifier) depend on assumptions (perfect verifier, sufficient sampling budget) that are favorable to the method; reported statistical uncertainty (seeds, error bars) is sparse in the main text.

Some arguments, e.g., the conjecture that GRPO's weighting inversion contributes to distribution sharpening, are explicitly left unproven and could overstate the theoretical story relative to what is actually established.
